title: Episode 52: GitHub Desktop
description: Using GitHub Desktop as an accessible alternative for cloning, branching, committing, and syncing.
concepts: Where GitHub Desktop fits among browser, VS Code, and CLI workflows
Creating branches, reviewing changes, committing, and pushing
Opening pull requests from GitHub Desktop
When to switch to VS Code or the browser
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're exploring GitHub Desktop, which is GitHub's free, open-source visual Git client for Windows and macOS.

[JAMIE]
So this is for someone who wants Git as its own app, separate from the code editor?

[ALEX]
Exactly. If VS Code's Source Control view feels too tucked inside the editor, GitHub Desktop gives you a dedicated space for cloning repositories, creating branches, reviewing changes, committing, syncing with GitHub, and handling a lot of the day-to-day Git work.

[JAMIE]
And it's worth saying: this appendix sits alongside the larger tool-choosing and Git-in-practice material, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. Think of this as a practical companion. If you're deciding between tools, or trying to build an accessible contribution workflow, GitHub Desktop is one strong option. And because this lesson is for blind and low-vision learners too, we'll keep noting what works well, what doesn't, and when another tool may be the better fit.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's orient to the full journey. We'll cover what GitHub Desktop can and cannot do, how to install it, how sign-in works, what the interface looks like, cloning, branching, staging and committing, pushing and pulling, syncing a fork, resolving conflicts, viewing history, cherry-picking, stashing, undoing changes, accessibility notes, and then when to use Desktop versus VS Code versus the Git command line.

[JAMIE]
So not just a sales pitch for the app.

[ALEX]
Not at all. More like: here is the tool, here are its boundaries, and here is how to use it wisely.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
A good place to start is scope. GitHub Desktop supports the everyday workflow most contributors use most days.

[JAMIE]
What counts as everyday workflow here?

[ALEX]
Cloning repositories from GitHub. Creating, switching, and deleting branches. Staging files, and even staging individual lines or hunks inside a file. Writing commit messages and committing. Pushing and pulling. Opening a pull request, though that part sends you to GitHub.com in your browser. It also supports merge conflict resolution with a visual editor, viewing commit history and diffs, cherry-picking commits from one branch to another, stashing and restoring uncommitted changes, undoing commits, and discarding changes.

[JAMIE]
That is a lot. For many people, that really is the whole routine.

[ALEX]
It is. But there are important limits. GitHub Desktop does not expose everything Git can do.

[JAMIE]
Such as the scary advanced stuff?

[ALEX]
Some of the advanced, powerful, and sometimes risky operations, yes. In the Desktop user interface, you do not get interactive rebase, so no visual equivalent of git rebase dash i. You also do not get git bisect, git clean, creating annotated tags, or commit signing with GPG or SSH from the UI.

[JAMIE]
So if I need those, I leave GitHub Desktop?

[ALEX]
You use the terminal, or sometimes VS Code's terminal. And GitHub Desktop helps with that by offering Repository, then Open in Terminal, or on Windows Open in Command Prompt, so you land in the correct repository folder immediately.

[JAMIE]
That's a nice bridge. You're not trapped in the GUI.

[ALEX]
Right. And for accessibility, that's significant. For screen reader users, Desktop handles a lot of core tasks through keyboard-friendly controls and standard text inputs, especially the commit message fields. For low-vision users, system zoom, display scaling, and high-contrast operating system themes matter a lot. And if the diff colors are hard to distinguish, opening the repository or diff in VS Code can give you more theme control.

[JAMIE]
And for sighted users, the three-panel layout gives a quick snapshot: files on one side, diff on the other, commit area below.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Okay, let's install it.

[ALEX]
On Windows, the recommended command-line install is winget install GitHub.GitHubDesktop.

[JAMIE]
So if someone already uses Winget, that's quick.

[ALEX]
Yes. The direct-download option is also simple: go to desktop dot github dot com, choose Download for Windows, run the installer, and it installs and launches automatically.

[JAMIE]
And on a Mac?

[ALEX]
If you use Homebrew, brew install dash dash cask github. Or go to the same website, choose Download for macOS, open the downloaded zip file, and drag GitHub Desktop into your Applications folder.

[JAMIE]
And Linux?

[ALEX]
No official Linux support for GitHub Desktop. Linux users should generally use VS Code's Source Control panel or the Git CLI.

[JAMIE]
That's important not to gloss over.

[ALEX]
Absolutely.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Once it's installed, what does sign-in look like? Do we need to manage personal access tokens or SSH keys?

[ALEX]
For normal GitHub.com use, no. GitHub Desktop uses browser-based OAuth sign-in. On first launch, you open GitHub Desktop, choose Sign in to GitHub.com, your browser opens to GitHub's authorization page, you sign in if needed, authorize GitHub Desktop, then return to the app.

[JAMIE]
And after that?

[ALEX]
The app stores credentials securely in the system keychain, so you usually won't be prompted for your password again.

[JAMIE]
What if someone uses GitHub Enterprise or an organization-hosted server?

[ALEX]
Then they choose Sign in to GitHub Enterprise Server and enter the server URL for that organization.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's build a mental model of the interface. GitHub Desktop has three main visual areas, plus a commit area.

[JAMIE]
Talk me through it as if I can't see the screen clearly.

[ALEX]
At the top is the toolbar. On the left is the Current Repository control, which lets you switch among local repositories you've opened in GitHub Desktop. Near the middle is Current Branch, which opens the branch selector. On the right is the sync control, usually labeled Fetch origin, Pull origin, or Push origin depending on state.

[JAMIE]
So the top bar answers three questions: which repo, which branch, and what's my sync status?

[ALEX]
Perfectly said. Then in the left panel you'll usually see either the Changes tab or the History tab. Changes lists uncommitted work. History lists past commits. The larger main area to the right shows either file diffs or commit details depending on what you've selected. And near the bottom left is the commit area with a Summary field, optional Description field, and a commit button that usually says something like Commit to main or Commit to feature slash name.

[JAMIE]
That sounds fairly structured.

[ALEX]
It is. For keyboard users and screen reader users, that structure matters. You can tab among the major regions. The branch selector behaves like a searchable dropdown: type to filter, use arrow keys to move, press Enter to select. The commit button is announced with the target branch name.

[JAMIE]
And for low-vision users?

[ALEX]
The toolbar stays fixed at the top, which helps. Increasing operating-system display scaling enlarges the interface proportionally. And the Changes and History tabs are clearly separated in the left panel. For sighted users, one useful cue is that the sync button changes icon or label to show whether you're fetching, pushing, or pulling.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's clone a repository. What's the easiest path?

[ALEX]
Often from GitHub.com. On a repository page, use the Code button and choose Open with GitHub Desktop. That launches the app with the repository URL already filled in. You choose the local folder where the repository should live, then activate Clone.

[JAMIE]
And if I want to stay inside the app?

[ALEX]
Use the clone shortcut: Control Shift O on Windows, Command Shift O on macOS. Then choose either the GitHub.com tab to browse repositories connected to your account, or the URL tab to paste any repository URL. Pick the local path and choose Clone.

[JAMIE]
The source also mentioned a GitHub CLI alternative.

[ALEX]
Yes. If you're comfortable in the terminal, you can run gh repo clone owner slash repo-name, and after that open the repository in GitHub Desktop with the github command followed by the path to the repo.

[JAMIE]
So Desktop can be the main tool or just one tool in a mixed workflow.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now we've got a cloned repository. Branches are next, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. Branching is one of the most common tasks. To create a new branch, open the Current Branch menu, choose the option to create a new branch, type the branch name, and confirm. GitHub Desktop will create it based on your current branch and switch you to it.

[JAMIE]
So I'm not just naming it. I'm also choosing the branch I branch from, whether explicitly or implicitly.

[ALEX]
Right. Usually it's based on whatever branch you're currently on, often main. To switch to an existing branch, open the same branch selector, type to filter if needed, move to the desired branch, and select it.

[JAMIE]
What if I have uncommitted changes and try to switch?

[ALEX]
GitHub Desktop may prompt you depending on whether the changes can safely move with you. In practice, if you're unsure, commit your work or stash it before switching branches. We'll talk about stashing later.

[JAMIE]
And deleting a branch?

[ALEX]
You generally switch away from the branch first, then use the branch menu to delete it. Deleting a branch removes the branch reference, not the commits themselves if they still exist elsewhere, but it's still something to do thoughtfully.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's get into the heart of daily Git work: staging and committing.

[JAMIE]
This is where people often blur concepts together. What does GitHub Desktop help us see clearly?

[ALEX]
It makes the review step very concrete. In the Changes tab, the left side lists modified, added, and deleted files. Selecting a file shows its diff in the main pane, so you can inspect exactly what changed before committing.

[JAMIE]
So reviewing changes is not optional busywork. It's how you confirm what you're about to record.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Then comes staging. In GitHub Desktop, files in the Changes list usually have checkboxes. Checked means staged for the next commit. Unchecked means leave it out.

[JAMIE]
That's a very approachable model.

[ALEX]
It is. And it gets better: you can often stage individual lines or hunks within a file. That means if one file contains two unrelated edits, you may be able to commit only the part relevant to your current task.

[JAMIE]
Can you explain hunk in plain language?

[ALEX]
A hunk is a chunk of nearby changed lines shown together in a diff. It's larger than a single line, smaller than the whole file. GitHub Desktop can let you include only certain chunks, or sometimes individual lines, to keep commits focused.

[JAMIE]
That helps create cleaner history.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Once staged, you write the commit message. The Summary field is the short title of the commit. The Description field is optional extra detail. Then you activate the commit button.

[JAMIE]
Any guidance on writing that summary?

[ALEX]
Make it specific and useful. For example, not update stuff, but fix broken heading navigation in README. The summary should help your future self and collaborators understand intent quickly.

[JAMIE]
And the source specifically notes that these fields are standard editable text inputs, which is good for screen reader support.

[ALEX]
Yes, that's an important accessibility detail.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
After committing locally, we need to sync with GitHub.

[ALEX]
Right. GitHub Desktop combines several related actions into the sync area at the top right. Fetch checks the remote for updates without changing your local branch. Pull fetches and then brings remote changes into your local branch. Push sends your local commits to GitHub.

[JAMIE]
Let's separate those carefully. What does fetch do for a cautious learner?

[ALEX]
Fetch is the safe look-before-you-touch option. It checks whether the remote has new commits and updates GitHub Desktop's awareness of that state, but it does not merge those commits into your current branch.

[JAMIE]
So if I just want to know whether anything changed upstream, fetch first.

[ALEX]
Exactly. If there are commits on GitHub that your local branch doesn't have, the app may then offer Pull origin. If you have local commits not yet on GitHub, it offers Push origin.

[JAMIE]
And if both sides changed?

[ALEX]
You may fetch, then pull, possibly followed later by push if you also have local work. The exact label can vary, but the conceptual model stays the same.

[JAMIE]
The source also calls out keyboard shortcuts here.

[ALEX]
Yes. The important lesson is not memorizing every shortcut, but knowing that the app supports keyboard access for clone and other common actions, and that sync operations are available through both toolbar controls and menus. If you're a keyboard-first user, it's worth exploring the menu bar on your platform to learn the exact commands GitHub Desktop exposes.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Fork workflows are really common in open source. How does syncing your fork fit into GitHub Desktop?

[ALEX]
If you've forked a repository, you usually have two remotes conceptually: your fork on GitHub, commonly called origin, and the original project repository, often called upstream. Syncing your fork means bringing changes from upstream into your local copy, and often later into your fork as well.

[JAMIE]
And if upstream isn't set yet?

[ALEX]
You need to configure the upstream remote. The appendix specifically notes setting up the upstream remote if it isn't already there. GitHub Desktop can help with common fork workflows, but there are times when checking or adding remotes may be clearer in the CLI.

[JAMIE]
So the conceptual requirement is: know where your branch is pulling from and where it's pushing to.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Without that, fork syncing becomes confusing fast.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's visit the part people dread: merge conflicts.

[ALEX]
Yes, but they become less scary once you understand them. A merge conflict happens when Git cannot automatically reconcile competing changes, often because the same lines were changed in different ways on different branches.

[JAMIE]
What does GitHub Desktop do when that happens?

[ALEX]
It will tell you there are conflicts and guide you into resolving them, often by opening the conflicted files in your editor or a visual resolution flow. The step-by-step idea is: identify the conflicted files, open and inspect them, choose which content to keep or combine, remove the conflict markers if you're editing manually, save the file, and mark the conflict as resolved.

[JAMIE]
Then what?

[ALEX]
After resolving in your editor, return to GitHub Desktop. Review the now-resolved changes, commit the merge or conflict resolution, and continue syncing as needed.

[JAMIE]
So Desktop is part coordinator, part visual assistant, but the actual text editing may happen in VS Code or another editor.

[ALEX]
Precisely. And for blind users in particular, editing conflict markers in a familiar text editor like VS Code may be much more accessible than relying on a highly visual merge interface.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Once you've worked for a while, history becomes important.

[JAMIE]
Not just what changed, but when and why.

[ALEX]
Exactly. In the History tab, GitHub Desktop shows the commit timeline for the current repository or branch context. You can navigate through commits, select one, and inspect its details and diff.

[JAMIE]
What about filtering commits?

[ALEX]
Filtering helps narrow history, often by searching commit messages, authors, or relevant content exposed by the interface. The key skill is using search or filtering to avoid reading an entire history when you're really looking for one fix or one person's work.

[JAMIE]
And a specific file's history?

[ALEX]
You can view the history related to a particular file, which is very useful when you want to know who changed one document, script, or configuration file over time.

[JAMIE]
Comparing branches is another big one.

[ALEX]
Yes. Comparing branches lets you inspect how one branch differs from another before merging, cherry-picking, or opening a pull request. It's a way to answer, what is unique here relative to there?

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Speaking of moving work across branches, let's talk about cherry-pick.

[ALEX]
Cherry-pick means taking a specific commit from one branch and applying it onto another branch, without merging the entire branch.

[JAMIE]
So if a bug fix exists on one branch and I need that exact fix on another, cherry-pick is the targeted move.

[ALEX]
Exactly. In GitHub Desktop, you typically find the commit in history, use the context menu or available command to cherry-pick it onto your current branch, and let Desktop apply it.

[JAMIE]
And if the commit doesn't apply cleanly?

[ALEX]
Then you get a conflict, just as you might during a merge. Resolve the conflicting files, save them, return to GitHub Desktop, and complete the process.

[JAMIE]
So cherry-pick is powerful, but it can still require careful conflict resolution.

[ALEX]
Yes.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now, stashing. This is one of those features people hear about before they really understand when to use it.

[ALEX]
A stash is a temporary shelf for uncommitted changes. You use it when you're in the middle of work but need a clean working tree, often to switch branches or handle an urgent task.

[JAMIE]
So it's like saying, hold this for me, I don't want to commit it yet.

[ALEX]
Exactly. In GitHub Desktop, you can stash your current changes, which removes them from the working view and returns the repository to a cleaner state. Later, you restore the stash to bring those changes back.

[JAMIE]
Any caution here?

[ALEX]
Yes. A stash is convenient, but it is easier to forget than a commit. If the work is meaningful and coherent, a real commit on a branch is often safer. Use stash for short-term interruption management, not as long-term storage.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's do undoing changes, because everyone eventually needs that.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. GitHub Desktop supports a few kinds of undo. One is undoing the last commit. That generally removes the commit while keeping the changed content available locally, so you can adjust it and recommit.

[JAMIE]
Useful if the message was wrong or the commit included something extra.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Another option is discarding changes to a file. That throws away the uncommitted edits in that file and restores it to its last committed state.

[JAMIE]
So that is destructive for uncommitted work.

[ALEX]
Yes, and learners should pause before using it. There's also discarding all changes, which wipes all current uncommitted modifications in the repository working tree. That's even more destructive.

[JAMIE]
So the rule is: understand whether you're undoing a commit or discarding uncommitted edits. Those are very different things.

[ALEX]
Exactly right.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's spend real time on accessibility and screen reader notes, because this appendix explicitly includes them.

[JAMIE]
Good. Start with what works well.

[ALEX]
GitHub Desktop does many core tasks through standard controls: buttons, text fields, lists, checkboxes, dropdowns. Keyboard navigation across major regions is generally workable. Commit message fields are standard edit fields. Cloning, branching, staging, committing, and pushing are all possible without depending purely on a mouse.

[JAMIE]
So for basic workflows, many users can absolutely use it.

[ALEX]
Yes. But there are limitations. Dense diff views can be harder to parse with a screen reader than a plain-text diff in an editor or terminal. Some visual branch comparisons or conflict-resolution flows may be less comfortable nonvisually. And if you're trying to perform something Desktop doesn't support, you'll need another tool anyway.

[JAMIE]
Let's make the Windows and macOS notes concrete.

[ALEX]
On Windows with NVDA or JAWS, tabbing through controls and interacting with standard input fields generally works well. The branch selector, commit fields, file list, and top toolbar are usually manageable. But reading complex diffs line by line may be slower than opening the file in VS Code, where screen reader navigation can be more granular.

[JAMIE]
And VoiceOver on macOS?

[ALEX]
Similar story. VoiceOver users can navigate the application's controls, but richly visual diff presentation may be less efficient than reviewing changed files in an editor with strong text navigation commands. The app is usable, but not always optimal for every task.

[JAMIE]
That leads naturally to the source's recommendation that VS Code may be a better accessible alternative in some cases.

[ALEX]
Exactly. VS Code often gives blind users better file editing, better direct text access to diffs and conflict markers, and a single environment for coding plus Git tasks. GitHub Desktop can still be helpful for branch switching, a visual overview, or quick commit workflows, but if accessibility friction rises, opening the repository in VS Code is often the better path.

[JAMIE]
And for low-vision users?

[ALEX]
Use system zoom, scaling, and high-contrast themes. Be aware that additions and deletions in diffs use green and red backgrounds, so if color distinction is hard, increase text size or open the same work in VS Code with a theme that gives you better contrast. On both platforms, operating-system display settings do a lot of the accessibility heavy lifting.

[JAMIE]
Can we summarize the learning-card style takeaways?

[ALEX]
Sure. For screen reader users: GitHub Desktop handles core workflows with keyboard-accessible controls, and you can jump to the terminal for unsupported operations. For low-vision users: system scaling and themes matter, and VS Code may offer better diff customization. For sighted users: the layout provides fast visual status awareness, especially the file status icons and sync indicators.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
So when should someone use GitHub Desktop instead of VS Code or the Git CLI?

[ALEX]
Use GitHub Desktop when you want a dedicated Git application with a clear visual workflow for cloning, branching, reviewing changes, and syncing. It's great when separating Git from coding helps reduce cognitive load.

[JAMIE]
Use VS Code when?

[ALEX]
When your work is tightly tied to editing files, reviewing text changes in context, resolving conflicts directly in source files, or when accessibility is better in your editor than in a standalone GUI. It's often the best all-in-one option.

[JAMIE]
And Git CLI?

[ALEX]
Use the Git command line when you need the full power of Git: interactive rebase, bisect, clean, advanced remote configuration, commit signing setups, scripts, automation, or simply the precision that comes from explicit commands.

[JAMIE]
So this isn't a competition with one winner.

[ALEX]
No. It's a toolkit. Many strong workflows combine all three. For example: clone and branch in GitHub Desktop, edit and resolve conflicts in VS Code, do advanced history surgery in the terminal.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we close, let's mention sources.

[ALEX]
The authoritative reference for this appendix is GitHub Desktop documentation from GitHub, along with broader GitHub Docs and related Git guidance. For accessibility framing, standard web accessibility guidance like WCAG is also relevant. If behavior changes in the app over time, always trust the current official GitHub Desktop docs over an older walkthrough.

[JAMIE]
That's a good reminder, especially because UI labels and workflows can evolve.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
So the big takeaway?

[ALEX]
GitHub Desktop covers a wide, practical slice of everyday Git work. It makes cloning, branching, staging, committing, syncing, history review, cherry-picking, stashing, and some conflict workflows approachable. It does not replace the terminal for advanced Git, and it does not always beat VS Code for accessibility or text-heavy tasks. But for many learners, especially those who want a purpose-built Git app, it's an excellent part of an accessible contribution workflow.

[JAMIE]
And the best way to learn it is probably to use it on a real repository.

[ALEX]
Yes. Clone something small, create a branch, make one change, review the diff, commit it, push it, and explore history. A calm, repeatable practice loop will teach you far more than memorizing buttons.

[JAMIE]
Perfect. That's GitHub Desktop.

[ALEX]
And we'll see you next time.

# Appendix H: GitHub Desktop
>
> **Episode coming soon:** GitHub Desktop - a conversational audio overview of this appendix. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Reference companion to:** [Chapter 01: Choose Your Tools](01-choose-your-tools.md) | Also relevant: [Chapter 14](14-git-in-practice.md)
>
> **Authoritative source:** [GitHub Desktop Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/desktop)

## A Visual Git Client for Every Workflow

> **Who this is for:** You want a dedicated graphical Git application — something separate from your code editor, with a clear visual interface for cloning, branching, committing, and managing pull requests. GitHub Desktop is a great fit if you prefer working with a purpose-built Git GUI, or if VS Code's Source Control panel feels too embedded in the editor for your workflow.
>
> GitHub Desktop is free, open source, and made by GitHub. It works on Windows and macOS.

---

## Table of Contents

1. [What GitHub Desktop Does (and Doesn't Do)](#1-what-github-desktop-does-and-doesnt-do)
2. [Installing GitHub Desktop](#2-installing-github-desktop)
3. [Signing In and Authentication](#3-signing-in-and-authentication)
4. [The Interface at a Glance](#4-the-interface-at-a-glance)
5. [Cloning a Repository](#5-cloning-a-repository)
6. [Creating and Switching Branches](#6-creating-and-switching-branches)
7. [Staging and Committing Changes](#7-staging-and-committing-changes)
8. [Push and Pull](#8-push-and-pull)
9. [Syncing Your Fork](#9-syncing-your-fork)
10. [Resolving Merge Conflicts](#10-resolving-merge-conflicts)
11. [Viewing History](#11-viewing-history)
12. [Cherry-Pick in GitHub Desktop](#12-cherry-pick-in-github-desktop)
13. [Stashing Changes](#13-stashing-changes)
14. [Undoing Changes](#14-undoing-changes)
15. [Accessibility and Screen Reader Notes](#15-accessibility-and-screen-reader-notes)
16. [GitHub Desktop vs VS Code vs Git CLI — When to Use Each](#16-github-desktop-vs-vs-code-vs-git-cli--when-to-use-each)

---

## 1. What GitHub Desktop Does (and Doesn't Do)

GitHub Desktop covers the everyday Git workflow that most contributors use on most days.

### What it supports

- Supported: Clone repositories from GitHub
- Supported: Create, switch, and delete branches
- Supported: Stage files (and individual lines/hunks within files)
- Supported: Write commit messages and commit
- Supported: Push and pull from GitHub
- Supported: Open pull requests (launches GitHub.com in your browser)
- Supported: Resolve merge conflicts with a visual editor
- Supported: View commit history and diffs
- Supported: Cherry-pick commits between branches
- Supported: Stash and restore uncommitted changes
- Supported: Undo commits and discard changes

### What it does not support (use Git CLI or VS Code terminal instead)

- Not supported in the GitHub Desktop UI: Interactive rebase (`git rebase -i`)
- Not supported in the GitHub Desktop UI: `git bisect`
- Not supported in the GitHub Desktop UI: `git clean`
- Not supported in the GitHub Desktop UI: Creating annotated tags
- Not supported in the GitHub Desktop UI: Commit signing (GPG/SSH)

For these operations, open the repository in your terminal directly from GitHub Desktop — **Repository → Open in Terminal** or **Repository → Open in Command Prompt** puts you in the right directory instantly.

### Learning Cards: What GitHub Desktop Does

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- GitHub Desktop handles cloning, branching, staging, committing, and pushing -- all accessible via keyboard and standard form controls
- For operations Desktop does not support (rebase, bisect, clean), use Repository then Open in Terminal to land in the right directory instantly
- All commit message fields are standard text inputs that screen readers announce as editable text

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- GitHub Desktop supports system-level zoom and high-contrast OS themes on both Windows and macOS
- The diff panel uses green and red backgrounds for additions and deletions -- pair these with font size adjustments in your OS display settings
- If the diff colors are hard to distinguish, open the same diff in VS Code via Repository then Open in VS Code for more theme options

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The three-panel layout (toolbar, file list, diff view) gives you a visual snapshot of your repository state at a glance
- Look for the badge count on the Fetch/Push button to see how many commits are waiting to push or pull
- The check mark, plus, and minus icons next to filenames show modified, added, and deleted status instantly

</details>

---

## 2. Installing GitHub Desktop

### Windows

**Option A: Winget (recommended)**

```bash
winget install GitHub.GitHubDesktop
```

**Option B: Direct download**

1. Go to [desktop.github.com](https://desktop.github.com)
2. Select **"Download for Windows"**
3. Run the installer — it installs and launches automatically

### macOS

**Option A: Homebrew**

```bash
brew install --cask github
```

**Option B: Direct download**

1. Go to [desktop.github.com](https://desktop.github.com)
2. Select **"Download for macOS"**
3. Open the downloaded `.zip`, drag **GitHub Desktop** to your Applications folder

> **Linux:** GitHub Desktop does not officially support Linux. Linux users should use VS Code's Source Control panel or the Git CLI.

---

## 3. Signing In and Authentication

GitHub Desktop uses **browser-based OAuth sign-in** — no tokens or SSH keys needed. It handles authentication for you automatically.

### Sign in on first launch

1. Open GitHub Desktop
2. Select **"Sign in to GitHub.com"**
3. Your browser opens to a GitHub authorization page — sign in with your GitHub account
4. Authorize GitHub Desktop when prompted
5. Switch back to GitHub Desktop — you're signed in

That's it. GitHub Desktop stores your credentials securely in the system keychain. You won't be asked for a password again.

> **If you use GitHub Enterprise or a GitHub organization:** Select **"Sign in to GitHub Enterprise Server"** and enter your organization's server URL.

---

## 4. The Interface at a Glance

GitHub Desktop has three main areas:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Toolbar: Current Repository ▾  |  Current Branch ▾  |  │
│                                    Fetch/Push button      │
├─────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┤
│                 │                                         │
│  Left panel:    │  Main area:                            │
│  Changes tab    │  File diff view                        │
│  (staged /      │  (what changed in the selected file)   │
│  unstaged)      │                                        │
│                 │                                         │
│  OR             │                                         │
│                 │                                         │
│  History tab    │  Commit detail / diff                  │
│  (past commits) │                                        │
│                 │                                         │

└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Key controls

| Element | What it does |
|---------|-------------|
| **Current Repository** (top left) | Switch between your cloned repos |
| **Current Branch** (top middle) | Switch branches, create new branches |
| **Fetch/Push button** (top right) | Sync with GitHub (fetch, push, pull) |
| **Changes tab** | Shows your uncommitted changes |
| **History tab** | Shows your commit history |
| **Summary field** (bottom left) | Where you type your commit message |
| **Commit button** (bottom left) | Commits staged changes |

### Learning Cards: The Desktop Interface

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Use `Tab` to move between the toolbar, file list, diff pane, and commit area -- each is a distinct focus region
- The branch selector is a searchable dropdown: type to filter, `Down Arrow` to navigate, `Enter` to select
- The commit button is announced as "Commit to [branch name]" -- press `Enter` to activate

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- The toolbar at the top stays fixed as you scroll -- repository name, branch, and sync button are always visible
- Increase your OS display scaling to enlarge all panels proportionally without breaking the layout
- The Changes and History tabs are side-by-side at the top of the left panel -- each tab label is clearly distinct

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The left panel toggles between Changes (uncommitted work) and History (past commits) -- click each tab to switch
- The main diff area updates when you select a different file in the left panel
- Look for the upward or downward arrow on the Fetch/Push button to see whether you need to push or pull

</details>

## 5. Cloning a Repository

### From GitHub.com

The easiest way is to go to the repository on GitHub.com and use the **Code** button:

1. On the repository page, activate **Code → Open with GitHub Desktop**
2. GitHub Desktop opens with a dialog confirming the URL
3. Choose where to save the repository on your computer
4. Select **"Clone"**

### From inside GitHub Desktop

1. Press `Ctrl+Shift+O` (Windows) or `Cmd+Shift+O` (macOS) — **"Clone a repository"**
2. Choose the **GitHub.com** tab to browse your own repositories, or the **URL** tab to paste any repo URL
3. Select or type the repository
4. Choose a local path
5. Select **"Clone"**

### GitHub CLI alternative

```bash
gh repo clone owner/repo-name
# Then open it in GitHub Desktop:
github /path/to/repo
```

---

## 6. Creating and Switching Branches

### Create a new branch

1. Click **Current Branch** in the toolbar (or press `Ctrl+Shift+N` / `Cmd+Shift+N`)
2. Type a name for your new branch
3. Select **"Create Branch"**
4. Choose whether to base it on the current branch or another — usually keep the default

GitHub Desktop switches to the new branch immediately.

### Switch to an existing branch

1. Click **Current Branch** in the toolbar
2. Type to search or scroll through the branch list
3. Click the branch name — GitHub Desktop switches and updates your files

### Delete a branch

1. Click **Current Branch** in the toolbar
2. Right-click the branch you want to delete
3. Select **"Delete..."**

> **Screen reader tip:** The branch selector is a dropdown that opens a searchable list. Screen readers announce the currently selected branch name in the toolbar. After switching, the branch name in the toolbar updates to confirm the switch.

---

## 7. Staging and Committing Changes

### Reviewing your changes

When you edit files in your editor and save them, GitHub Desktop automatically detects the changes and shows them in the **Changes** tab on the left.

- The **left panel** lists every changed file with a checkbox
- The **right panel** shows the diff for the selected file — red lines removed, green lines added

### Staging files

Every file with a checked checkbox will be included in your next commit.

- **Check all** — click the checkbox at the top of the list to stage everything
- **Uncheck** a file to exclude it from the commit (it stays as an uncommitted change)

### Staging individual lines (hunks)

If a file has multiple changes and you only want to commit some of them:

1. Select the file in the Changes list
2. In the diff view, **right-click** a line or block
3. Select **"Stage Line"** or **"Stage Hunk"** — only those lines get included in the commit

### Writing your commit message

1. In the **Summary** field at the bottom, type a short commit message (under 72 characters is ideal)
2. Optionally add a longer description in the **Description** field below it
3. Select **"Commit to [branch name]"** — your changes are committed locally

> **GitHub Copilot can help:** Not sure what to write? Open VS Code alongside GitHub Desktop, open Copilot Chat, and ask: *"Write a commit message for these changes: [describe what you changed]."* Or use the conventional commit format: `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`.

> **Screen reader tip (Windows, NVDA/JAWS):** The Summary and Description fields are standard text inputs — navigate to them with `Tab` and type normally. The commit button is announced as a button labelled "Commit to [branch name]."

---

## 8. Push and Pull

After committing, your changes are saved locally but not yet on GitHub. The **Fetch/Push** button in the top-right toolbar handles syncing.

### Pushing commits to GitHub

After committing, the button changes to **"Push origin"** with an upward arrow and the number of commits waiting.

- Click **"Push origin"** — your commits go to GitHub

### Pulling changes from GitHub

When collaborators have pushed new commits, the button shows **"Pull origin"** with a downward arrow.

- Click **"Pull origin"** — GitHub Desktop downloads the new commits and updates your local branch

### Fetching (checking without pulling)

- Click **"Fetch origin"** — GitHub Desktop checks for new commits and shows you the count, but doesn't update your files yet
- This is safe to do at any time — it's read-only

### Keyboard shortcuts

| Action | Windows | macOS |
|--------|---------|-------|
| Push / Pull / Fetch | `Ctrl+P` | `Cmd+P` |

---

## 9. Syncing Your Fork

If you forked a repository and the original upstream repo has new commits you want to bring in:

1. Go to **Branch → Merge into current branch...**
2. In the branch picker, switch to the **"Other branches"** tab
3. Select `upstream/main` (or `upstream/master`) — the upstream remote's default branch
4. Select **"Create a merge commit"**
5. Then push to your fork with **"Push origin"**

### Setting up the upstream remote (if not already there)

GitHub Desktop adds the upstream remote automatically when you clone a fork from GitHub.com. If it's missing:

1. Open the repository in terminal: **Repository → Open in Terminal**
2. Run:

```bash
git remote add upstream https://github.com/ORIGINAL-OWNER/ORIGINAL-REPO.git
git fetch upstream
```

1. Switch back to GitHub Desktop — it will now see the upstream branches

---

## 10. Resolving Merge Conflicts

When you pull from GitHub or merge a branch and there are conflicts, GitHub Desktop shows a dialog listing the conflicting files.

### Step by step

1. GitHub Desktop shows a **"Resolve conflicts before merging"** screen
2. Each conflicting file has two options next to it:
   - **"Open in [your editor]"** — opens the file with conflict markers for manual editing
   - **"Use mine"** / **"Use theirs"** — accept one entire side of the conflict without editing

3. For simple conflicts (one side is clearly right), use **"Use mine"** or **"Use theirs"**
4. For conflicts where you need to keep parts of both, select **"Open in [editor]"** and resolve manually

### After resolving in your editor

1. Save the file
2. Switch back to GitHub Desktop — the file moves from "Conflicting" to "Resolved"
3. Once all conflicts are resolved, select **"Continue merge"**

> **GitHub Copilot can help:** Open the conflicting file in VS Code alongside GitHub Desktop. Place your cursor inside a conflict region and open Copilot Chat (`Ctrl+Alt+I`, or **Chat: Open Chat** from the Command Palette if your keymap differs): *"Resolve this merge conflict - keep meaningful changes from both sides."* Copilot suggests a resolution; you review and save.

> **Screen reader tip:** The conflicts dialog lists files as a navigable list. Each file entry includes the action buttons ("Open in editor", "Use mine", "Use theirs"). Navigate with `Tab` between the file entries and buttons.

---

## 11. Viewing History

The **History** tab (next to the Changes tab in the left panel) shows every commit on the current branch.

### Navigating history

1. Click the **History** tab
2. Each commit appears as a row: author avatar, commit message, author name, and timestamp
3. Click any commit to see the full diff on the right — what changed in each file

### Filtering commits

Type in the **search field** above the commit list to filter by commit message, author, or SHA.

### Viewing a specific file's history

1. Right-click any file in your project (via the Files panel in the diff area)
2. Select **"Show in History"** — the commit list filters to only commits that touched that file

### Comparing branches

1. Click **History**
2. In the branch comparison bar above the commit list, switch to another branch
3. GitHub Desktop shows the commits that are different between your current branch and the selected branch

---

## 12. Cherry-Pick in GitHub Desktop

Cherry-pick lets you take a commit from another branch and apply it to your current branch — without merging the whole branch.

### How to cherry-pick

1. Switch to the **branch you want to copy the commit FROM** (the source branch)
2. Open the **History** tab
3. Find the commit you want to copy
4. **Right-click** the commit
5. Select **"Cherry-pick commit..."**
6. Choose the **destination branch** — the branch you want to apply the commit TO
7. GitHub Desktop applies the commit and switches to the destination branch

### If there's a conflict

GitHub Desktop shows the conflict resolution screen (same as merging). Resolve the conflicts in your editor, then switch back to GitHub Desktop to continue.

> **GitHub Copilot can help:** Before cherry-picking, open Copilot Chat and paste the commit diff: *"What does this commit do? Is it safe to cherry-pick onto a branch that doesn't have the surrounding context?"*

---

## 13. Stashing Changes

Stash saves your uncommitted changes temporarily so you can switch branches or pull without committing half-finished work.

### Stash your changes

1. Go to **Branch → Stash All Changes** (or press `Ctrl+Shift+H` / `Cmd+Shift+H`)
2. Your working directory reverts to the last commit
3. You can now switch branches safely

### Restore your stash

1. Switch back to the branch where you stashed
2. Go to **Branch → Pop Stash**
3. Your changes come back

> **Note:** GitHub Desktop supports one stash at a time per branch. For multiple stashes, use the Git CLI: `git stash list`, `git stash apply stash@{1}`. See [Chapter 14, Section 10](14-git-in-practice.md#10-stash-management) for the full stash guide.

---

## 14. Undoing Changes

### Undo the last commit

Go to **Edit → Undo Last Commit** (or press `Ctrl+Z` / `Cmd+Z` right after committing)

This is equivalent to `git reset --soft HEAD~1` — your changes come back as staged files. Nothing is lost.

### Discard changes to a file

In the **Changes** tab:

1. Right-click a file
2. Select **"Discard Changes..."**
3. Confirm the dialog — the file reverts to its last committed state

> **Warning:** Discarding changes cannot be undone. The changes are permanently deleted, not moved to trash.

### Discard all changes

1. Right-click anywhere in the Changes list
2. Select **"Discard All Changes..."**
3. Confirm — everything in your working directory reverts to the last commit

---

## 15. Accessibility and Screen Reader Notes

GitHub Desktop has partial screen reader support. Core workflows work well with keyboard navigation; some visual-only elements (like avatar images and some icons) don't have text equivalents.

### What works well

| Feature | Accessibility notes |
|---------|-------------------|
| Commit message fields | Standard text inputs, fully accessible |
| Branch selector | Searchable dropdown, keyboard navigable |
| File list (Changes/History) | Arrow keys to navigate, checkboxes announceable |
| Commit button | Labelled with branch name, activatable with `Enter` |
| Conflict resolution dialog | Buttons ("Use mine", "Use theirs") are labelled |
| Keyboard shortcut access | Most operations have keyboard shortcuts |

### What has limitations

| Feature | Limitation |
|---------|-----------|
| Diff view | The colored diff panel is partially accessible; individual lines may not be announced clearly on all platforms. **Workaround:** Open in VS Code for better diff navigation |
| File icons | Status icons (M for modified, A for added, D for deleted) may not always be announced — the filename is still readable |
| Context menus | Right-click context menus work via keyboard (`Shift+F10` on Windows; `Ctrl+Click` on macOS) |

### Windows — NVDA / JAWS

- Use `Tab` to move between panels; arrow keys within lists
- The commit summary field is reached with `Tab` after the file list
- Conflict dialogs are modal — screen reader focus moves into the dialog automatically

### macOS — VoiceOver

- Use `Tab` and `VO+Arrow` to navigate panels
- The diff view can be explored with `VO+Right` through the lines
- Branch selector opens a searchable popup — type to filter, `Down Arrow` to navigate, `Return` to select

### VS Code as a better accessible alternative

If screen reader navigation in GitHub Desktop is frustrating for a specific operation, VS Code's Source Control panel is often more accessible. The two tools complement each other — use whichever works best for the task at hand.

### Learning Cards: Desktop Accessibility

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Commit message fields, branch selector, and conflict resolution buttons are fully keyboard-accessible and announced
- The diff panel has partial screen reader support -- for difficult diffs, switch to VS Code's Accessible Diff Viewer (`F7` / `Alt+F2`)
- Use `Shift+F10` on Windows to open context menus via keyboard when right-click actions are needed

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- File status icons (M, A, D) are small -- increase OS scaling or watch for the filename and status text that accompany them
- The conflict resolution dialog uses labeled buttons ("Use mine", "Use theirs") that are easy to identify at any zoom level
- If diff colors are indistinguishable at your contrast settings, open the same file in VS Code for richer theme support

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The colored diff highlights (green for added, red for removed) are visible in the main panel as soon as you click a file
- Modal conflict dialogs appear front-and-center with clear action buttons -- no hunting required
- Keyboard shortcuts like `Ctrl+Shift+O` (Clone) and `Ctrl+Shift+N` (New Branch) speed up common workflows visually

</details>

---

## 16. GitHub Desktop vs VS Code vs Git CLI — When to Use Each

| Situation | Best tool |
|-----------|-----------|
| You want a clean visual overview of changes before committing | GitHub Desktop |
| You want to stage individual lines or hunks | GitHub Desktop or VS Code |
| You're doing complex operations (rebase, bisect, clean) | Git CLI (terminal) |
| You want the fastest screen-reader-friendly experience | Git CLI or VS Code terminal |
| You want to open a PR or manage issues without leaving your tool | VS Code (GitHub Pull Requests extension) |
| You want to manage multiple repos at once with a visual switcher | GitHub Desktop |
| You're doing quick commits mid-coding session | VS Code (Source Control panel — already open) |

GitHub Desktop, VS Code, and the Git CLI all talk to the same Git repository. You can switch between them freely — use GitHub Desktop to stage and commit, then open the terminal for a `git rebase -i`. They don't conflict.
